stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, paraphrasing the argument of A. Kent MacDougall (1992) as summarized in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 3. Post-1929 source: paraphrased, not quoted.
stimulus.text: Silver poured into Spain from Mexico and the Andes through the 1500s, yet most Spaniards grew poorer. Prices rose across Europe as more silver money circulated. The crown raised taxes more than fivefold to pay for the largest army in Europe, and borrowed heavily besides. A tiny class of landowners owned nearly all the land and had no reason to build workshops or factories; wool went to Holland to be made into cloth. The wealth arrived, and then it left again, spent on soldiers and interest.

stem: According to the passage, what best explains why the flood of American silver did not improve life for most Spaniards?

options.text: Spain received too little silver from the Americas to make any difference at home.
options.misconception: The passage says silver poured in; the problem was what Spain did with it, not how much arrived.

options.text: The crown invested the silver in Spanish farms, workshops, and new factories.
options.misconception: The passage says the opposite: landowners had no reason to modernize, and wool went to Holland to be made into cloth.

options.text: The crown spent the silver on armies and interest while prices rose at home.
Silver led Spain to withdraw from European wars and disband its large armies.
options.misconception: The passage says the opposite: silver funded the largest army in Europe and an arms race.

instruction: Answer from the stimulus and stem only. Pick one option. Do not open the question file.
